1.title: Prompting Fundamentals
1.text: Welcome to Module one: Prompting Fundamentals. This module covers prompting fundamentals. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. What makes a prompt effective: goal, context, audience, format and constraints. The core moves: be clear and direct, give the why, show examples, add a role, separate instructions from material. How to prompt for business tasks (reports, emails, plans) and technical tasks (formulas, scripts, data cleanup) without being a developer. How to ask Claude to ask you questions and to admit uncertainty.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedarbrook's Vague Request
1.text: Our running case is Cedarbrook Outfitters. Cedarbrook's Vague Request. A marketing coordinator types: "Write a product description for the Ridge tent.". Claude returns a generic, four hundred-word paragraph that sounds like every other tent. The coordinator then rewrites the request with audience, tone, length, key facts and format and gets text the team can use.

1.title: The Anatomy of an Effective Prompt
1.text: The Anatomy of an Effective Prompt. The figure shows this: An effective prompt states the goal, the context, the audience, the format, the constraints and, when useful, an example. Think of Claude as a brilliant new colleague who knows nothing about your company. The more precisely you explain the job, the better the result.

1.title: The Anatomy of an Effective Prompt, continued
1.text: The Anatomy of an Effective Prompt, continued. Goal. What to state: The task and what a good result is. Example: "Write a ninety-word product description that makes a family choose this tent". Context. What to state: Background, purpose, the why. Example: "It is for the spring catalog; our customers are first-time campers". Audience. What to state: Who will read it. Example: "Parents with young children; no jargon". Format. What to state: Structure, length, tone. Example: "One headline, three bullets, one closing sentence; friendly tone". Constraints. What to state: Must and must-not. Example: "Mention the four point two lb weight; no claims about waterproofing ratings". Example. What to state: A sample of the style you want. Example: "Here is last year's description for the Trail tent".

1.title: The Anatomy of an Effective Prompt, continued
1.text: The Anatomy of an Effective Prompt, continued. Key test: Show your prompt to a colleague with no background. If they would be confused about what to do, Claude will be too. Exam tip: A weak result is most often a weak prompt, not a weak tool. The first fix is to add the missing goal, context, audience, format or constraint.

1.title: Be clear and direct
1.text: Be clear and direct. Say exactly what you want, including extras. If you want more than the bare minimum ("include charts and a summary"), ask for it: Claude does not guess ambitious scope from a short request. Give sequential steps (numbered list) when order or completeness matters. State what to do rather than only what to avoid: "write in plain sentences" works better than "don't use jargon" alone.

1.title: Give the reason
1.text: Give the reason. Explain why a rule exists and Claude can apply it sensibly. "Never use ellipses.". "This text is read aloud by a speech tool, so avoid ellipses, which it cannot pronounce.". "Keep it short.". "Support agents read this on a phone between calls, so keep it under sixty words.".

1.title: Use examples
1.text: Use examples. Examples are among the most reliable ways to steer tone, format and structure. Use three to five examples that are relevant (match the real task), diverse (cover different cases) and clearly marked as examples. One example can be enough for a simple format; no example is fine for a plain task.

1.title: Separate instructions from material
1.text: Separate instructions from material. Put pasted documents, emails or data in clearly labeled blocks (for example, tags such as less than email greater than... less than or email greater than or lines like "Document starts or Document ends") so Claude does not confuse your instructions with the content to work on. With long documents, put the documents first and the question and instructions last.

1.title: Give Claude a role
1.text: Give Claude a role. A single sentence such as "You are a careful financial analyst for a retail company" focuses tone and approach. A role helps style and focus; it does not add knowledge Claude lacks and does not replace checking the output.

1.title: Let Claude ask and admit doubt
1.text: Let Claude ask and admit doubt. "Before you start, ask me up to three questions if anything is unclear" avoids a wrong first draft. "If you are not sure, say so instead of guessing" and "quote the source line you used" reduce invented details (Module three).

1.title: Let Claude ask and admit doubt, continued
1.text: Let Claude ask and admit doubt, continued. The figure shows this: The same task as a vague prompt and as a strong prompt: the strong one names the goal, audience, format and constraints. Exam tip: When a question gives two prompts and asks which will work better, pick the one with specific context, audience, format and constraints, not the shorter one and not the one that just asks for "your best work".

1.title: Let Claude ask and admit doubt, continued
1.text: Let Claude ask and admit doubt, continued. Menu names, features and model behavior change; the prompting principles above do not. Current guidance is on Anthropic's prompting best-practices page.

1.title: Prompts for Business and Technical Tasks
1.text: Prompts for Business and Technical Tasks. Drafting (email, report, post). Prompt moves that work: Name audience, tone, length; give key facts; ask for a draft you will edit. Cedarbrook example: "Draft a one hundred twenty-word apology email to a customer whose order is five days late; calm, specific, offer a ten percent credit". Summarizing. Prompt moves that work: State the reader and the purpose; ask for key decisions and open questions. Cedarbrook example: "Summarize this twenty-page supplier contract for the finance director: costs, deadlines, penalties".

1.title: Prompts for Business and Technical Tasks, continued
1.text: Prompts for Business and Technical Tasks, continued. Analysis. Prompt moves that work: Provide the data; define the question and the output; ask for the assumptions. Cedarbrook example: "From this C S V of weekly sales, which three categories grew fastest? Show the figures you used". Technical help for non-developers. Prompt moves that work: Say your tool and your goal; paste the data shape; ask for the steps and an explanation. Cedarbrook example: "In Google Sheets, write a formula to total column C only where column A says 'West'; explain it in one line".

2.title: Prompts for Business and Technical Tasks, continued
2.text: Prompts for Business and Technical Tasks, continued. Structuring information. Prompt moves that work: Name the output format (table, checklist, Jason (Java Script Object Notation)-like list) and the fields. Cedarbrook example: "Turn these meeting notes into a table: action, owner, due date". For technical tasks you still state the goal, the tool or version and an example of the input; then test what Claude gives you on a small sample. Scripts, formulas and macros that Claude writes must be tested before they touch real data or go to I T (Module fifteen). Exam tip: "Business and technical tasks" does not mean building software. It means using Claude for formulas, data cleanup, templates and simple automation, and escalating real integration work to a Developer.

2.title: Common Mistakes
2.text: Common Mistakes. One-line request with no audience. State the reader and purpose. Mixing five tasks in one sentence. One clear task, or numbered steps (Module two). Pasting a document with no instructions about it. Say what to do with it, and put the question after it. Assuming Claude knows your company. Give facts, or put them in a Project (Module eleven). Asking "make it better". Say how: shorter, friendlier, more formal, with numbers. Treating the first answer as final. Review and iterate (Module two).

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Six elements: Goal, context, audience, format, constraints, example. Key test: Would a new colleague with no background understand the prompt? Reasons: Explain why a rule exists. Examples: three to five, relevant, diverse, labeled. Long inputs: Documents first, question last; label each block. Role: Focuses tone; adds no knowledge. Clarify: Invite questions; ask Claude to say when unsure. Technical tasks: State goal, tool, sample data; test on a small sample.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A coordinator asks Claude: "Write an email about the delay." The draft is generic. What is the best next step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The prompt lacks context and constraints; adding them is the most reliable improvement.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Which prompt is most likely to give a usable result? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. It names the reader, the format and the focus.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A team wants consistent product descriptions in the house style. Which technique helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer tone and format.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A user pastes a thirty-page report and then types a question in the last line. Why does this order help? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. For long inputs, place the documents first and the instructions or question at the end.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. An analyst's rule says "Never use ellipses," and Claude sometimes uses them. What change is most effective? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Giving the reason lets Claude apply the rule sensibly.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Select two. Which two additions make a prompt for a customer reply more effective? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and C. Audience and tone, and a good example, give Claude what it needs; urgency or praise adds no information.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. A team lead wants Claude to avoid a wrong first draft when the brief is incomplete. Which instruction helps? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Inviting questions surfaces the missing context before the draft.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. A project manager needs a Google Sheets formula but has no coding background. What is the best approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Technical help still needs clear context, and the result must be tested on a small sample.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Which statement about assigning Claude a role is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Roles shape style and focus; accuracy still has to be verified.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all nine answers. Question one: B. Question two: A. Question three: C. Question four: D. Question five: A. Question six: B and C. Question seven: C. Question eight: D. Question nine: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
